transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-02-09 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Rachel Park (Redwood CSM); Priya Kapoor (CTO, Goldcrest), Ben Yates (Infra Lead), Sara Lim (Security), Tom Novak (ML Eng)

Summary:
Short intake to understand Goldcrest's need for dedicated (reserved) GPU capacity, isolation requirements, burst strategy and expected scaling profile. Customer leaning toward Dedicated for latency predictability and data isolation; exploring Private on-prem option for compliance if cost permits.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and bottlenecks (inference on k8s + spot instances)
- Isolation needs: tenant fencing, VPC/private control plane, KMS integration
- Burst model: prewarm/warm pools, soft bursts vs sustained throughput, failover to Hosted
- SLOs: p50/p95 latency targets, planned QPS, concurrency per model
- Compliance: SOC2 scope, audit logs retention, SSO/SAML, RBAC

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, Luis is our systems SE, Rachel's our CSM. Priya, would you like to kick off with a bit of context on Goldcrest?
[00:12] Priya (CTO): Sure, yeah. Thanks. So Goldcrest is building a real‑time insights product for financial news. We run an ensemble of models — some smaller rerankers, and a 13B style generative model for summaries. Currently we run inference on k8s with GPU spot nodes, and it's... um, it's been a bit flaky under spikes.
[00:28] Ben (Infra): Yeah, spot preemption kills the warm KV caches and then we see big latency spikes. We're evaluating reserved GPUs so we can guarantee p95 and reduce cold starts.
[00:38] Maya (AE): Perfect, that's exactly why many customers pick Dedicated. Luis, maybe high level on how Redwood Dedicated treats warm pools and prewarming?
[00:45] Luis (SE): Yeah. Short answer — we support reserved node pools with configurable warm pools and a hotprewarm strategy. For large models we keep a warm KV cache and can keep a small number of GPUs prewarmed to reduce first‑token latencies. Our runtime also supports automatic prefix caching to cut downstream cost. But, important tradeoffs: more warm nodes = higher reserved cost.
[01:05] Tom (ML Eng): When you say KV cache, is that per‑model shard? How much memory are we talking for a 13B with 1024 prefix?
[01:12] Luis (SE): Good q. It depends on model tokenizer and kv compression; rough ballpark is 8–12GB of GPU RAM for KV per concurrent session for 13B at 1k context if not quantized. If you run quantized variants you can drop that. We'll run the exact numbers in the sim.
[01:26] Priya (CTO): Our SLO goals are p50 < 80ms and p95 < 350ms for summary generation at median prompt lengths. We see baseline QPS of ~30 QPS, bursts up to 300 QPS during market opens.
[01:39] Maya (AE): That's helpful — are those QPS numbers per region or global?
[01:42] Ben (Infra): Global, but mostly US‑east and EU‑west peak windows. We want isolation so other tenants on the same pool can't noisy neighbor us.
[01:51] Sara (Security): From security, main asks: VPC private control plane, customer‑managed KMS/HSM, audit logs retention for 1 year, SOC2 attestation, and SSO via SAML with SCIM provisioning.
[02:03] Luis (SE): All pretty standard. Dedicated supports VPC peering/private control plane and KMS integrations; we can map audit log retention tiers. SAML + SCIM for enterprise accounts is supported. For SOC2, we have a pack of security docs we can share.
[02:15] Priya (CTO): Cool. Another question: how does Redwood help with graceful degradation? During a massive spike we could fall back to a smaller generative model or to hosted endpoints.
[02:24] Luis (SE): Exactly. Smart routing lets you define fallback policies — e.g., if 13B latency climbs beyond threshold, route to a 7B distilled model or to Hosted low‑cost pool. That requires you to codify quality regress criteria and acceptance thresholds.
[02:36] Tom (ML Eng): We do have a tolerable quality delta for certain noncritical widgets. Rewrites and summaries are okay to be lower quality briefly.
[02:42] Maya (AE): Timeline wise, when are you hoping to have a pilot or PoC?
[02:45] Priya (CTO): Ideally pilot in 6 weeks. Execs want a 90‑day runway for cost justification. So pilot in early March would be ideal.
[02:54] Maya (AE): Great, we can do an initial capacity sim + cost estimate quickly. Luis, flag any immediate constraints?
[02:58] Luis (SE): Two items: 1) we need a representative traffic trace and some prompt examples to simulate prefix distributions; 2) we need to know whether customer wants per‑tenant node fencing vs soft isolation (GPU pool with tenant quotas).
[03:10] Ben (Infra): For us, per‑tenant fencing is preferred for regulatory reasons on some customers; others could be soft isolated. Can Redwood do dedicated tenants on the same reserved pool but fenced?
[03:20] Luis (SE): Yes — we have dedicated node groups (hardware isolated) or multi‑tenant reserved pools with strict cgroup and scheduler isolation. Dedicated node groups give the strongest isolation and preemption immunity, but cost more.
[03:30] Sara (Security): Do you support hardware attestations for on‑prem? We might consider Private if we have to run on our own metal because of client contracts.
[03:37] Luis (SE): Redwood Private includes an on‑prem package that supports HSM/KMS integration and optional offline attestations; it's more involved operationally and requires an initial deployment window. We can map the cost/ops delta in the proposal.
[03:49] Priya (CTO): Another concern — how do you handle burst billing? If we reserve nodes and then burst beyond the reserved count, is there an automatic overtime charge or do we fall back to hosted instances?
[03:59] Maya (AE): We offer two patterns: capacity bursting on our hosted fleet billed at on‑demand rates, or strict enforced throttling with queueing. Contracts can be a hybrid: reserved baseline + pay‑as‑you‑go burst. We can model both.
[04:11] Ben (Infra): For the fallbacks, will the data cross tenant boundaries? Data residency is important. If bursts go to Hosted, will logs or requests pass through shared systems?
[04:20] Luis (SE): If you allow Hosted burst, we can configure it to keep inference and payloads within specified regions and apply data handling rules; however Hosted inevitably means shared infra. For the strictest compliance we recommend Private or fully isolated Dedicated node groups.
[04:34] Tom (ML Eng): For model versions and rollouts — we need pinning so we don't accidentally roll new weights during production.
[04:39] Luis (SE): You can pin model versions per route and use canary rollouts with automatic rollback on regression metrics. We also integrate with Redwood Optimize to recommend quantization and batching profiles for your workload.
[04:51] Priya (CTO): Costs: ballpark numbers please — how much does a reserved 8‑GPU node pool run monthly?
[04:57] Maya (AE): We'll send detailed pricing. Ballpark — depends on GPU type and commitment term. For example, an 8xA100‑configured reserved node across a monthly commit is materially cheaper than on‑demand; exact numbers in the pricing sheet. We'll include options for prewarmed hot pools and for hybrid burst billing.
[05:12] Sara (Security): We need to review your SOC2 report and pen test summary before moving forward.
[05:16] Rachel (CSM): We'll attach those docs and our compliance pack to the follow up email.
[05:20] Ben (Infra): Operational question — what's the typical time to spin up a reserved node pool vs a Private on‑prem install?
[05:26] Luis (SE): Reserved node pools can be provisioned in our Dedicated region in hours to a day depending on capacity. Private on‑prem is typically 4–8 weeks including network setup and validations.
[05:36] Priya (CTO): Good to know. For pilot scope I think we want: 1) reserve a small Dedicated pool for US‑east, 2) warm pool for 2 GPUs for the 13B model, 3) fallback to 7B hosted in EU for noncritical windows.
[05:49] Maya (AE): Sounds like a clear pilot. We'll scope cost for that exact config. Luis, next steps on the sim?
[05:54] Luis (SE): I'll run burst simulations with the provided trace once they share it; I'll produce expected p95s and token cost for 13B/7B/quantized variants. Aim to have that by 2026‑02‑13.
[06:06] Priya (CTO): We'll send the trace and 20 prompts by COB 2026‑02‑12.
[06:10] Tom (ML Eng): Quick nit — what's the infra for KV cache persistence? If preemption occurs we lose caches; do you do long lived persistent caches between sessions?
[06:18] Luis (SE): KV is in GPU memory for low latency. We persist prefix embeddings to a fast backing store (NVMe) in some configs to speed rehydrate, but nothing beats warm GPU state. So reserved warm nodes are recommended.
[06:31] Maya (AE): Any other open concerns?
[06:33] Sara (Security): Just one: RBAC granularity for operations — we need separation between infra ops and model deployment teams.
[06:39] Luis (SE): RBAC supports role separation down to route and model level; you'll be able to restrict deploy permissions.
[06:44] Priya (CTO): Great.
[06:46] Maya (AE): Recap: Redwood to send Dedicated pricing + security docs; SE run burst sim once traffic trace arrives; customer to send trace and prompts; target pilot early March. We'll sync after SE posts results.
[06:58] Ben (Infra): Sounds good.
[07:00] Priya (CTO): Thanks, all.

End of transcript.
